description: The discrete Fourier transform family and its spectrum-shifting helpers, polynomial and signal convolution and deconvolution, and the difference-equation and 2-D filtering functions available in core MATLAB without the Signal Processing Toolbox.

tools.name: fft
tools.description: Computes the discrete Fourier transform with a fast Fourier transform algorithm, along the first non-singleton dimension or a dimension you choose. Zero-padding or truncating to n points is done with the second argument, which is how you control frequency resolution. Use it for spectrum analysis, fast convolution and filtering in the frequency domain.
tools.usage:
Y = fft(X)
Y = fft(X, n)
Y = fft(X, n, dim)

parameters.name: X
parameters.description: Signal, real or complex; columns are transformed for a matrix.

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Transform length; pads with zeros or truncates.

tools.notes: MATLAB does not normalize the forward transform, so divide by n to get amplitudes. Output bin 1 is DC and the spectrum of a real signal is conjugate symmetric, so only the first half carries unique information.

tools.name: ifft
tools.description: Computes the inverse discrete Fourier transform, including the 1/n normalization that `fft` omits. The 'symmetric' option tells MATLAB to treat the input as conjugate symmetric and return a strictly real result, which avoids tiny imaginary residues. Use it to return to the time domain after frequency-domain processing.
tools.usage:
X = ifft(Y)
X = ifft(Y, n)
X = ifft(Y, n, dim)
X = ifft(___, symflag)
tools.notes: Using 'symmetric' is both faster and cleaner than calling `real(ifft(...))`. If you modify a spectrum by hand, keep the conjugate symmetry or the inverse transform will not be real.

tools.name: fft2
tools.description: Computes the two-dimensional discrete Fourier transform, equivalent to an FFT along each dimension in turn. Use it for image spectra, 2-D filtering, and correlation of images via the frequency domain. Padding to a larger size with the m and n arguments both increases resolution and allows linear rather than circular convolution.
tools.usage:
Y = fft2(X)
Y = fft2(X, m, n)

parameters.name: X
parameters.description: 2-D array or a stack of 2-D pages.

parameters.name: m, n
parameters.description: Number of rows and columns in the transform, with zero padding or truncation.

tools.notes: The zero-frequency component sits at index (1,1); use `fftshift` to move it to the centre for display. For a page-wise transform of a 3-D stack, fft2 operates on the first two dimensions.

tools.name: ifft2
tools.description: Computes the two-dimensional inverse discrete Fourier transform with normalization, optionally forcing a real result with the 'symmetric' flag. Use it to complete a frequency-domain image filtering pipeline. Padding arguments let you interpolate an image by transforming, zero padding and inverting.
tools.usage:
X = ifft2(Y)
X = ifft2(Y, m, n)
X = ifft2(___, symflag)
tools.notes: Building a frequency mask by hand requires respecting conjugate symmetry; otherwise use 'symmetric' and accept that the imaginary part is discarded.

tools.name: fftn
tools.description: Computes the N-dimensional discrete Fourier transform of an array. Use it for volumetric data, for multidimensional convolution, and for any transform beyond two dimensions. The size argument pads or truncates each dimension independently.

parameters.name: sz
parameters.description: Vector of transform sizes, one per dimension.

tools.notes: Memory grows with the product of the padded sizes, so padding a 3-D volume to the next power of two can be expensive. `ifftn` is the inverse.

tools.name: ifftn
tools.description: Computes the N-dimensional inverse discrete Fourier transform with normalization, with an optional 'symmetric' flag for real results. Use it to finish an N-dimensional frequency-domain operation such as fast volumetric convolution. Sizes can be specified to pad or truncate.
tools.usage:
X = ifftn(Y)
X = ifftn(Y, sz)
X = ifftn(___, symflag)
tools.notes: Multiplying transforms performs circular convolution; pad both arrays to at least the sum of their sizes minus one to obtain linear convolution.

tools.name: fftshift
tools.description: Rearranges a Fourier transform by swapping half-spaces so that the zero-frequency component moves to the centre of the array. Use it before plotting spectra so that negative frequencies appear on the left, and for building centred frequency masks. For vectors it swaps the halves; for matrices it swaps quadrants.

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Dimension to shift; all dimensions by default.

tools.notes: For odd-length input, fftshift and `ifftshift` are not the same operation; always use ifftshift to undo a fftshift. The frequency axis after shifting is `(-n/2:n/2-1)*Fs/n` for even n.

tools.name: ifftshift
tools.description: Undoes the effect of `fftshift`, moving the zero-frequency component from the centre back to the first element. Use it after constructing a centred frequency-domain filter and before multiplying it with an unshifted FFT. It is the exact inverse of fftshift for both even and odd lengths.
tools.notes: For even-length arrays fftshift and ifftshift happen to be identical, which hides bugs that then appear on odd lengths. Always pair fftshift with ifftshift.

tools.name: nextpow2
tools.description: Returns the exponent of the smallest power of two that is at least the absolute value of the input. Use it to choose an FFT length that is a power of two, which historically gives the fastest transform and is still a good default for zero padding. Combine it with `pow2` or 2^ to get the length itself.
tools.notes: Modern FFTW-based implementations handle composite lengths well, so padding to a power of two is no longer always faster; measure with `timeit` if performance matters. Padding also changes the frequency grid.

tools.name: fftw
tools.description: Controls the FFTW planning method MATLAB uses to compute fast Fourier transforms, and saves or restores tuning information. Setting a more exhaustive planner makes the first transform of a given size slower but subsequent transforms of that size faster. Use it when a program performs a very large number of transforms of the same length.
tools.usage:
method = fftw('planner')
fftw('planner', method)
str = fftw('dwisdom')
fftw('dwisdom', str)
fftw('swisdom', str)

parameters.name: 'dwisdom'/'swisdom'
parameters.description: Get or set the accumulated double or single precision wisdom string.

tools.notes: Wisdom is lost when MATLAB exits unless you save the string and restore it at startup. Planning modes beyond 'measure' can take a long time for large or unusual sizes.

tools.name: conv
tools.description: Computes the convolution of two vectors, which is also polynomial multiplication when the vectors are coefficient lists. The shape option selects the full result, the central part the same length as the first input, or only the fully overlapping part. Use it for FIR filtering, moving-window weighting and multiplying polynomials.
tools.usage:
w = conv(u, v)
w = conv(u, v, shape)
tools.notes: The 'full' result has length numel(u)+numel(v)-1. For very long signals, frequency-domain multiplication with `fft` is far faster, and `conv` already switches strategy internally for large inputs.

tools.name: conv2
tools.description: Computes the two-dimensional convolution of two matrices, the basic operation behind image filtering, blurring and edge detection. Shape options control whether the output is the full convolution, the same size as the input, or only the fully overlapping region. A separable kernel can be applied as two vectors for a significant speed-up.
tools.usage:
C = conv2(A, B)
C = conv2(A, B, shape)
C = conv2(u, v, A, shape)

parameters.name: u, v
parameters.description: Column and row vectors of a separable kernel.

tools.notes: Convolution flips the kernel; `filter2` correlates instead, which matters for asymmetric kernels such as Sobel operators. Image Processing Toolbox `imfilter` adds border handling options that conv2 lacks.

tools.name: convn
tools.description: Computes the N-dimensional convolution of two arrays, generalizing conv and conv2 to volumes and higher-dimensional data. Use it for 3-D smoothing of volumetric data and for multidimensional filter kernels. Shape options work as they do in conv2.
tools.usage:
C = convn(A, B)
C = convn(A, B, shape)
tools.notes: Direct N-D convolution cost grows as the product of the array and kernel sizes; for large kernels use `fftn` multiplication instead. Separable kernels can be applied one dimension at a time for large savings.

tools.name: deconv
tools.description: Performs polynomial long division, returning the quotient and remainder, which is the deconvolution of two sequences. Use it to divide polynomials, to recover a filter input when the impulse response is known exactly, and to split a transfer function. It is exact for polynomial division but very sensitive to noise when used to invert a measured filter.
tools.notes: Deconvolution of noisy measured data amplifies noise enormously; regularized approaches such as Wiener filtering are needed in practice. The remainder tells you how far v is from being an exact factor.

tools.name: filter
tools.description: Applies a rational transfer function filter defined by numerator b and denominator a using a direct form II transposed difference equation. It handles both FIR (a = 1) and IIR filters, and can carry filter state across calls for block processing. Use it for causal filtering of signals and for simulating discrete-time systems.
tools.usage:
y = filter(b, a, x)
y = filter(b, a, x, zi)
y = filter(b, a, x, zi, dim)
[y, zf] = filter(___)

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Denominator coefficients; a(1) must be nonzero and the result is normalized by it.

tools.notes: filter is causal and introduces phase delay; Signal Processing Toolbox `filtfilt` removes the delay by filtering forwards and backwards. Carrying zf between blocks is essential for streaming data.

tools.name: filter2
tools.description: Applies a two-dimensional FIR filter by correlation rather than convolution, which means the kernel is not flipped. It is implemented on top of `conv2` and shares the same shape options. Use it for image smoothing and for template matching where correlation is the natural operation.
tools.usage:
Y = filter2(H, X)
Y = filter2(H, X, shape)
tools.notes: filter2 defaults to 'same' output while conv2 defaults to 'full'. Because it correlates, asymmetric kernels behave as most image-processing texts describe without manual flipping.

tools.name: detrend
tools.description: Removes a constant, linear or higher-order polynomial trend from data, optionally in piecewise segments defined by breakpoints. Use it before spectral analysis to avoid leakage from a slowly varying baseline, and to isolate fluctuations from a drifting sensor. Since R2019b it also supports continuity constraints and returning the trend itself.
tools.usage:
y = detrend(x)
y = detrend(x, n)
y = detrend(x, n, bp)
y = detrend(___, nanflag)
[y, trend] = detrend(___)

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Trend degree: 0 for mean removal, 1 for linear (default), or higher.

parameters.name: 'Continuous'
parameters.description: true (default) to force the piecewise trend to be continuous.

tools.notes: Detrending before an FFT reduces spectral leakage from the DC and near-DC components dramatically. A high-order polynomial trend can absorb genuine signal, so keep n small.

tools.name: interpft
tools.description: Resamples a periodic signal to a new length using the Fourier method, which is exact for band-limited periodic data. Use it to upsample or downsample a waveform without designing a filter, for example to increase the resolution of a periodic simulation result. The signal is assumed periodic over the sample window.
tools.usage:
y = interpft(x, n)
y = interpft(x, n, dim)

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Number of samples in the output.

tools.notes: Non-periodic data produces ringing at the ends because the method wraps around. For non-periodic resampling use `interp1` or Signal Processing Toolbox `resample`.
